newsitem.title: USA: U.S. products outlook - further pullback seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. products outlook - further pullback seen.

text.p: U.S. petroleum products traders agreed Saddam Hussein will loom large this week as the driving market fundamental, eclipsing normal supply and demand dynamics.
But as both the Iraq crisis and the tight U.S. distillate stocks stories fade as heavily-hyped factors in the market, traders see further pullback in products prices in the week ahead.
Spot New York Harbor heating oil and gasoline futures were leading the market lower Monday, slipping by more than one cent by midday.

Cash New York heat was offered at 67 cents a gallon. It had hit almost 69 cents a gallon last Thursday, pricey indeed for this time of year although still well below the 80-cent mark reached April 11.

New York Harbor unleaded gasoline briefly jumped two cents a gallon Thursday but retreated Friday back to the 64-cent range as Iraq tensions began to ease, well below its 1996 peak on April 26 of almost 75 cents a gallon.
Players expressed surprise that heating oil differentials barely budged last week despite low U.S. stocks of only 48 million barrels -- 19 million shy of last year.
"I thought heat would have found support at two cents below NYMEX futures," one Gulf trader said, noting Gulf material had held stable about 2.50 cents below the NYMEX print.
But Toronto trader Bob Macminn said he believed the talk of low heating oil stocks has been overhyped.
"There's a tremendous amount of speculative length attracted to the market," Macminn said, adding he expected a "washout" in heating oil to begin in the next few weeks.
"Heat could pull back to 60 cents a gallon," he said, as refineries continue to switch over from gasoline to heating oil and boost domestic inventories.
Rising NYMEX prices last week also fueled a rally in Midwest spot prices, but plentiful stocks in the region were expected to exert downward pressure on basis this week.
Traders reported some discounting emerged last week at the wholesale level, which should translate into weaker prices on barrels for delivery in late September.

"I think we're going to be discounting quite a bit, which will drive basis lower," one Kansas City, Mo., trader said. "Wholesale values are going to come off, (and) there's already been some discounting."
Traders said gasoline prices on the West Coast should hold their ground this week even if NYMEX heads moderately lower.
Problems at several key refineries in Los Angeles promised to keep buyers in the hunt for supplies.
"They're going to be buying for at least another week," one trader said, referring to Arco, Chevron, and Mobil plants, stricken by planned and unexpected outages.
Arco last week said a coker at its Carson, Calif., refinery would stay shut for about 10 more days.
The disabled unit forced crude runs to drop from 260,000 barrels per day to 190,000
